    BPC-157 price per mg: what shops charge, and what the number hides.

    Peptide Chooser editorial team. Checked 30 Oct 2026.

    Short answer

    Price per mg is the price of a vial divided by the amount of peptide the shop says is in it; it says nothing about what is really in the vial. BPC-157 is not FDA approved for any use. On 30 Oct 2026 the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) said it does not intend to act against licensed pharmacies that compound it for one patient on a prescription, under 10 conditions. That is not FDA approval, and research-use vials are still not approved for use in people.1

    What do shops charge per mg?

    We show the price per mg once our price crawl has BPC-157 listings. The middle price is the one in the middle when all listings are put in order, so a few very cheap or very dear vials do not pull it.

    We crawl the shops' own pages for the price and the amount on the label. We do not sell anything.

    How do we work out the price per mg?

    We take the listed price and divide it by the amount of BPC-157 the label gives. A pack of ten 10 mg vials counts as 100 mg. Blends, listings with no amount and prices outside $0.01 to $100 per mg, which are almost always a typing error on the shop's page, are left out of the range.

    Prices change. Our Fresh prices check counts a shop's prices as current when our crawl saw one in the last 30 days, and each row below shows the day we last saw that price.2

    Which shops are in our window?

    We show the shops once our price crawl has BPC-157 listings.

    Why is price per mg not the whole story?

    • Vial size. A big vial or a pack of vials often has a lower price per mg. Compare the same size, or compare the whole price.
    • The amount is the shop's word. The mg on the label is what the shop says. Only a test of that batch shows what is in the vial.
    • Blends. A vial that mixes BPC-157 with TB-500 or another peptide rarely says how much of each is in it, so we leave blends out of the price per mg.
    • Shipping and extras. The price we see is the listed price, before shipping, taxes or a coupon.

    What does a lab report cover?

    A certificate of analysis (COA) is a lab's test of one batch: how pure it was and, if tested, how much peptide was in the vial. It covers that batch only, tested once, and it is worth more when a lab outside the shop did the test. Our guide How to read a peptide COA shows each line.

    What does a low price leave out?

    A low price per mg does not mean a good buy. BPC-157 is not approved for use in people, and the FDA found little or no information on its safety in people.3 The cheapest vial and the dearest one share that.

    Our five checks (Lab reports, No FDA letter, Found in a state registry, Legal pages, Fresh prices) tell you facts about the shop, not about the vial.2 Our BPC-157 page has its FDA status and the letters that name it, and our guide Is BPC-157 legal? explains the July 2026 review.

    We do not give doses. None of this is medical advice.
